title: Phorvex — Applications: State, Decisions & Resources
description: Per-app availability, uptime, resource usage, decision value and actual defensive dispatch. The legacy risk-named metric reports P1 candidate coverage; zero does not establish that no attack occurred.

panels.title: Apps monitored
panels.description: Namespaces in scope that currently run at least one pod.

panels.title: Workloads fully available
panels.description: Deployments whose available replicas equal the desired count. Sourced from kube-state-metrics, not from pod phase — a Running pod that fails its readiness probe is NOT available and is excluded here.

panels.title: Degraded workloads
panels.description: Deployments running below their desired replica count.

panels.title: Apps attacked (risk > 0, last 15m)
panels.description: Namespaces with a current P1 decision whose considered or selected action has positive recon-fact coverage value. Zero may mean no eligible covering action; it is not an all-clear or an attack detector.

panels.title: Actuations (1h)
panels.description: Defensive moves actually enacted against the cluster in the last hour.

panels.title: Kill switch
panels.description: When engaged the operator DECIDES but never acts. A quiet board with the kill switch on means suppression, not safety.

panels.title: Candidate coverage & decisions — by app name
Apps under attack — peak candidate coverage, last 15m
panels.description: One tile per namespace with positive P1 candidate coverage value. Empty means no positive covering candidate is reported; it does not show that no attack occurred.

panels.title: Decision per app — what Phorvex chose, and whether it acted
panels.description: Every (app, action) pair the engine is deciding, at what rate, and whether the move was SELECTED. `noop` is a real decision: the engine looked and deliberately chose to spend nothing. Actuated is what actually reached the cluster — a selected move with no actuation means the kill switch, dryRun, or a broken actuator.

panels.title: 🛡 Defenses chosen and fired per app (last 15m)
panels.description: One tile per app against which Phorvex ACTUATED a defensive move in the last 15 minutes — the results half of the fire-an-attack loop. Fire an attack from the launcher and the target app appears here by name the moment the operator acts. Empty means no defensive action has fired recently, not that nothing was attacked (an attack the engine judged not worth a move leaves no actuation).

defaults.noValue: No defense fired in the last 15m

panels.title: Decisions per app over time (by action)
panels.description: Decision rate split by app and chosen action. A flat all-noop band is a calm cluster; any other action appearing means the engine is responding to something.

panels.title: Defensive moves ACTUATED per app
panels.description: Moves that actually reached the cluster, in 10-minute buckets. Compare with the decision panel to the left: decisions that never become actuations are the gap worth investigating.

panels.title: 🔒 Quarantined pods (isolated from their Service)
panels.description: Pods whose ownerReference has been taken over by an AdaptiveMovingTargetDefense CR. A quarantine strips the pod's labels, so it leaves the Service endpoints and its controller's replica count while still reporting Ready. It keeps running and keeps costing capacity, but serves nothing. Nothing releases it automatically — a quarantine here is permanent until someone clears it.

panels.title: Per-app state — availability, uptime, resources, threat
Application state (one row per app)
panels.description: Every app in one row. Availability comes from kube-state-metrics, uptime from the oldest running pod, resources from cAdvisor, and candidate coverage/blast radius from Phorvex. Coverage value is not a direct attack signal; zero can mean no eligible covering action.

properties.value: Distinct pod IPs behind a Service and marked ready. Lower than 'Pods ready' means a pod is running and healthy but taking no traffic — normally an AMTD quarantine, which strips the pod's Service labels.

panels.title: Decision value & context — not an attack detector
Candidate coverage value
panels.description: P1 recon-fact coverage value of the considered or selected action. This legacy risk-named metric is zero when no candidate is chosen; zero does not prove no attack or no trusted event.

panels.title: Blast radius — context: how much is reachable from here
panels.description: Decayed reachability out to 3 hops, normalised against the worst pod in the cluster. High blast radius is potential impact context, not evidence that an attack is present.

panels.title: Net benefit — would acting be worth its cost
panels.description: Candidate coverage value minus the current cost coefficient times estimated cost. Positive value is economic context, not proof that an action was selected or actuated.

panels.title: Decision rate vs actuation rate
panels.description: Decisions are what the engine concluded; actuations are what it actually did to the cluster. A wide and persistent gap means moves are being selected but never enacted — either the kill switch, dryRun, or a broken actuator.

panels.title: Exposure clock — seconds since each variable last changed
panels.description: How long an attacker-visible variable has stayed constant. Moving-target defence exists to keep this number down; a monotonically rising line means nothing has been rotated and the attacker's knowledge is still valid.

panels.title: Availability ratio per workload
panels.description: available replicas / desired replicas. 1.0 is fully available. This is the same quantity Phorvex's own availability-floor feasibility law reasons about, so a dip here explains a refused defensive move.

panels.title: App uptime (oldest running pod)
panels.description: Age of the longest-running pod per app. A sawtooth here is rotation or crash-looping; the Restarts column in the table above tells you which.

panels.title: Container restarts (24h)
panels.description: Restarts are the cheapest early warning of an unhealthy app.

panels.title: Pods ready vs total
panels.description: A gap between the two lines is pods that exist but are not serving traffic.

panels.title: CPU cores per app
panels.description: Actual consumption from cAdvisor, not requests. Compare with the limits panel to spot apps that are throttled.

panels.title: Memory working set per app
panels.description: Working set is what the OOM killer actually looks at — a better signal than RSS or cache-inclusive usage.

panels.title: Network throughput per app
panels.description: Received above the axis, transmitted below. These are the exact two counters Phorvex's physics stage reads for its flow-conservation residual: bytes in with almost nothing out, or data leaving with no matching requests, is the exfiltration shape it looks for.

panels.title: TCP connections per app
panels.description: From the standalone cAdvisor DaemonSet — the kubelet does not expose this series. It feeds Phorvex's fan-out residual: connections far exceeding the request rate is the signature of lateral probing or C2 multiplexing.

panels.title: LLM serving — latency percentiles, throughput, GPU
End-to-end request latency percentiles
panels.description: Computed from vLLM's own histogram buckets, not sampled or estimated. NaN means no requests were served in the window — an idle model, not a fault.

panels.title: Time to first token percentiles
panels.description: For a streaming model this is what a user actually perceives as latency; end-to-end conflates it with how long the answer happened to be.

panels.title: Token throughput
panels.description: Recorded from vllm:generation_tokens_total. Phorvex reads this same series as TokensPerSec; when it was absent the engine computed a phantom throughput collapse the moment GPU utilisation crossed 50%.

panels.title: Queue depth (requests waiting)
panels.description: Feeds the queue term of the physics residual: depth large relative to arrival rate means work is piling up faster than it drains.

panels.title: GPU utilisation & memory
panels.description: From dcgm-exporter. GPU utilisation above 50% with token throughput at zero is the exact condition behind the phantom-collapse false positive.
